newsitem.title: USA: Christian Science Church to sell radio operations.
newsitem.headline: Christian Science Church to sell radio operations.

text.p: The Christian Science Church will sell Monitor Radio, a news network used by more than 200 public radio stations in the United States, church officials said Wednesday.
The church, which also publishes The Chrisian Science Monitor newspaper, said it was confident a buyer can be found. It said it would continue to operate Monitor Radio until at least the end of June.
"Our church must balance its desire to serve a radio audience with the need to support its worldwide healing ministry and to strengthen our newspaper," Monitor editor David Cook said in a statement.
Monitor Radio had sponsors to defray operating expenses but was still costing the church $8 million a year, an official said.

The Boston-headquartered chuch said it will also sell or lease its two shortwave radio stations, WSHB in Cypress Creek, S.C., and KHBI on Saipan in the western Pacific, but will continue to offer programing through other shortwave broadcasters.

Monitor Radio, which began in January 1984, was the second largest provider of news programing to public stations behind National Public Radio. It was heard by an estimated 1.1 million people each week.

"We've played a very important role keeping NPR's feet to the fire," said Sue Schardt, the marketing and development manager who said NPR offered weekend and midday news programming only after Monitor Radio did it.
Cook said "several potential buyers" have come forward and the church was looking for a buyer who will keep Monitor Radio's staff and offer a similar service to public radio stations.
Among the potential buyers was Public Radio International, PRI, a rival of NPR, which handled Monitor Radio's distribution to individual U.S. public radio stations, Monitor officials said.
The announcement caught many public radio programmers by surprise. Stations often use Monitor Radio to supplement NPR's well-known news programs; "All Things Considered" and "Morning Edition."
"We're still in shock," said Maine Public Radio manager Charles Beck. "The unknown is who Monitor Radio gets sold to and what (the programming) ends up looking like."
Cook said the Monitor will remain "a constructive force in radio news," but said future radio efforts will be "more modest in scale" and "will have to give promise of being self supporting."
The church in 1992 shut down its short-lived cable television network, The Monitor Channel, and sold a Boston television station because of financial problems.
